scenarios.title: Fernhill Veterinary Group
scenarios.stem:
Fernhill Veterinary Group runs three vet surgeries. Receptionists book appointments and take payments, and vets record each animal's treatment on a shared client records system. The records hold pet owners' names, addresses, phone numbers and payment card details.

Last month a receptionist clicked a link in an email that claimed to be from a pet insurance company and typed in her login details. The IT support company also found that:
• several staff keep their passwords on sticky notes under their keyboards
• a PC in the back office still runs an old version of Windows that no longer gets updates
• the server is kept in a storeroom that is not locked.

scenarios.title: Kestrel Logistics
scenarios.stem:
Kestrel Logistics is a delivery company with 120 staff, a head office and two depots. Drivers use tablets to record deliveries, and office staff use laptops to manage customer accounts, which include customers' names, addresses and payment details.

A manager recently left an unencrypted laptop holding customer data on a train. It was never found. The directors have asked the IT manager, Priya, to write proper cyber security documentation for the company.

scenarios.title: Lumen Design Studio
scenarios.stem:
Lumen Design Studio is moving into a new two-floor office.

• The first floor has 12 desktop PCs for the designers and a file server that stores large design files.
• The ground floor has a reception desk with one PC and a printer, and a meeting room where visiting clients use guest Wi-Fi.
• Clients log in to a client portal on Lumen's website to download their designs.
• Three designers work from home two days a week using company laptops and need to reach the file server.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Insurance
scenarios.stem:
Alex, a claims handler at Brightwater Insurance, resigned last week. The HR manager suspects that Alex copied customer records before leaving. Network logs show large uploads from Alex's laptop to a personal cloud storage account on Alex's last day.

Alex's work laptop and company mobile phone have been handed in. Brightwater may take legal action, so any evidence must be able to stand up to scrutiny.

questions.question: Give **two** internal threats to Fernhill's client data, other than an employee clicking a link in an email.
traps: "internal": the threat must come from someone inside the organisation. Hackers and viruses on their own are external.
"other than … clicking a link in an email": the scenario's own example earns nothing.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Accidentally deleting or overwriting client records
Deliberate sabotage by an unhappy employee, e.g. deleting or changing records
Sharing or writing down passwords (e.g. sticky notes)
Leaving a PC logged in or unlocked where clients can see or use it
Accidental disclosure, e.g. emailing a client's details to the wrong person
Losing a laptop, phone or USB stick that holds client data
Plugging in personal USB devices or installing unauthorised software
An employee stealing client data, e.g. card details
accept: Any other threat that comes from a member of staff
reject: Clicking a link in an email (excluded by the question)
External threats with no staff involvement, e.g. "hackers" or "viruses"

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Staff writing their passwords on sticky notes
2. A receptionist accidentally deleting a client's records

questions.question: Give **two** physical security measures Fernhill could use to protect its server.
traps: "physical": software such as a firewall or antivirus is not a physical measure.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Lock the storeroom / keep the server in a locked room or cabinet
Keypad or swipe-card entry to the room
Biometric lock, e.g. fingerprint
CCTV covering the storeroom door
Intruder alarm
Sign-in book / only named staff allowed in
Cable lock or locked server rack
accept: Any other physical measure that protects the server
reject: Software or logical measures: passwords, firewall, antivirus, encryption

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Keep the server in a locked cabinet
2. Fit a keypad lock to the storeroom door

questions.question: Explain **two** impacts on Fernhill if a ransomware attack encrypted its client records system.
traps: Each impact needs a consequence for Fernhill to earn the second mark. "They would lose money" on its own is only an identification.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying an impact and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to Fernhill), up to 4 marks.
points: Operational loss / surgeries cannot run normally
because vets cannot see animals' medical histories or appointments, so treatment is delayed or cancelled
Financial loss
from cancelled appointments, paying specialists to recover the system, or paying a ransom
Reputational loss / loss of client trust
so pet owners may move to another vet, reducing future income
Legal consequences / GDPR breach
if personal data was accessed it must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours and Fernhill could be fined
Permanent loss of records
if there are no working backups, vaccination and treatment histories cannot be recovered
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense
reject: "Hacking" or "data stolen" with no impact on Fernhill

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Vets would not be able to open animals' records, so appointments would be delayed or cancelled and pets might not get the right treatment.
2. Clients could lose trust in Fernhill after hearing their details were caught up in an attack, so they may take their pets to another vet.

questions.question: Explain **two** vulnerabilities in Fernhill's current set-up, other than the receptionist clicking the link.
traps: Use the scenario. The question rewards spotting the weaknesses the IT support company found, not a general list.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a vulnerability and 1 more for explaining how it could be exploited, up to 4 marks.
points: Passwords written on sticky notes
so anyone at the desk, including clients or cleaners, could read them and log in as that member of staff
The back-office PC runs an unsupported version of Windows
so known security holes are never patched and malware can exploit them
The server is in an unlocked storeroom
so anyone could steal or damage it, or plug in a device to copy data
Payment card details are stored in the records system
which makes Fernhill a valuable target and increases the damage from a breach
accept: Any other genuine vulnerability linked to the scenario
reject: The receptionist clicking the link (excluded by the question)

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Staff keep passwords on sticky notes under their keyboards, so a client at the reception desk could read one and log in to the records system.
2. The back-office PC runs an old version of Windows that no longer gets updates, so attackers can use known security holes to install malware.

questions.question: Describe how multi-factor authentication (MFA) would protect Fernhill's client records.
traps: Two passwords are not two factors. The factors must be different types.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each point, up to 4 marks.
points: The user must give two or more different types of evidence (factors) to log in
Something you know, e.g. a password or PIN
Something you have, e.g. a code sent to a phone, an authenticator app or a smart card
Something you are, e.g. a fingerprint or face scan
A stolen or phished password on its own is no longer enough to log in
One-time codes expire after a short time, so they cannot be reused
A login attempt can alert the real user that someone has their password
accept: Examples linked to Fernhill, e.g. a receptionist approving a login on her phone
reject: Two passwords / a password and a security question (same factor type)
"Makes it more secure" on its own

questions.modelAnswer: MFA means staff must prove who they are in two different ways before the records system lets them in. As well as something they know, such as a password, they need something they have, such as a one-time code from an authenticator app on their phone. The code changes every 30 seconds, so it cannot be reused. If a receptionist's password is phished again, the attacker still cannot log in without her phone.

questions.question: Discuss the methods, other than multi-factor authentication, that Fernhill could use to reduce the risk of further social engineering attacks.
traps: "other than multi-factor authentication": anything about MFA earns nothing.
Discuss means consider both sides: the benefit of each method and a drawback or limitation.

markScheme.focus: Methods other than MFA, applied to staff at a vet surgery being tricked by emails and calls.
indicative: Staff training on spotting phishing: fake sender addresses, urgent requests, checking a link before clicking. Needs time away from clients and regular refreshers
Simulated phishing emails to test staff and target extra training. Can upset staff if handled badly
Email filtering / spam and anti-phishing filters to stop most phishing reaching inboxes. May block genuine emails from insurers
An internet and email use policy that staff sign, with clear rules. Only works if it is enforced
A procedure to check unusual requests, e.g. phone the insurance company on a known number
A no-blame reporting process so staff report a mistake straight away and damage is limited
Access controls / least privilege so a tricked receptionist's account cannot reach everything
Keeping software patched and anti-malware up to date, to limit the damage if a link is clicked
Drawbacks weighed: cost, staff time, false positives, relies on people following rules
reject: Multi-factor authentication (excluded by the question)

questions.modelAnswer:
Fernhill's biggest weakness is its staff, so training is the most important method. Receptionists could be shown how to spot phishing emails, for example by checking the real sender address and being suspicious of urgent requests to log in. This would have helped in last month's attack. However, training takes staff away from the front desk and has to be repeated, because people forget and attacks change.

Fernhill could also use email filtering to block known phishing emails before staff ever see them. This reduces how often staff have to make the right decision, although some phishing still gets through and genuine emails from insurers might be blocked.

An email and internet use policy would make the rules clear, such as never entering a password from a link in an email, and tell staff how to report anything suspicious. A no-blame reporting process matters, because a receptionist who reports a mistake quickly lets the IT company reset the password before data is taken. A policy only works if managers check it is being followed.

Finally, access controls would limit the damage. If receptionists can only see appointments and payments, a phished receptionist account cannot reach full clinical records.

questions.context: Priya is writing rules for staff who use company laptops outside the office.
questions.question: Give **two** rules that should be included in Kestrel's policy for staff using company laptops outside the office.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Laptops must use full-disk encryption
Never leave a laptop unattended in public or in a vehicle
Lock the screen when away from it / use a privacy screen in public
Only connect to company systems through the VPN on public Wi-Fi
Report a lost or stolen laptop immediately, and to whom
No use by family or friends / work use only
Keep the laptop's software and security updates installed
Use a strong password and MFA to log in
accept: Any other sensible rule for laptops used off-site
reject: Rules that only apply inside the office

questions.modelAnswer:
1. All laptops must be encrypted.
2. A lost or stolen laptop must be reported to the IT manager straight away.

questions.question: Explain **two** reasons why Kestrel should carry out regular security audits.
traps: An audit checks what is actually happening. Reasons about writing the policy in the first place miss the point.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a reason and 1 more for expanding it, up to 4 marks.
points: To check staff are following the policies
so problems such as unencrypted laptops are found before they cause another breach
To find new vulnerabilities, e.g. missing patches or open ports
so they can be fixed before attackers exploit them
To review user accounts and access rights
so accounts of staff who have left are removed and insider risk is reduced
To show compliance with GDPR
giving evidence to the ICO and customers that Kestrel takes data protection seriously
To measure whether security is improving
as the Check stage of Plan-Do-Check-Act, so policies can be updated
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense
reject: "To make it more secure" on its own

questions.modelAnswer:
1. An audit checks whether staff are actually following the rules, for example whether every laptop is encrypted, so gaps are found before another laptop is lost.
2. An audit can find accounts that belong to staff who have left, so they can be disabled before they are misused.

questions.question: Explain **two** benefits to Kestrel of having a data protection policy.
traps: Benefits to Kestrel. Make each one specific to a company holding customer addresses and payment details.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a benefit and 1 more for expanding it, up to 4 marks.
points: Helps Kestrel comply with GDPR
reducing the risk of fines or legal action after a breach like the lost laptop
Staff know how to handle personal data
so mistakes such as carrying unencrypted customer data are less likely
Sets out how long data is kept and when it is deleted
so less personal data is at risk if a device is lost
Explains how and when to report a breach
so the ICO is told within 72 hours
Builds customer trust
so businesses are more willing to use Kestrel for deliveries
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense

questions.modelAnswer:
1. The policy tells staff exactly how customer data must be stored and carried, so mistakes like taking unencrypted data out on a laptop are less likely.
2. It explains how to report a data breach, so Priya can tell the ICO within 72 hours and Kestrel is less likely to be fined.

questions.question: Explain **two** items that should be included in Kestrel's disaster recovery policy.
traps: Disaster recovery is about getting systems back after a major event (fire, flood, ransomware), not about preventing attacks.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying an item and 1 more for explaining why it is needed, up to 4 marks.
points: A list of critical systems in order of priority
so the delivery tracking system is restored first and drivers can keep working
Recovery time and recovery point targets
so everyone knows how quickly systems must be back and how much data can be lost
Roles, responsibilities and contact details
so staff know who does what and there is no confusion during a disaster
An alternative site or equipment, e.g. a depot or cloud service
so the business can carry on if head office cannot be used
Where backups are kept and how to restore them
so data can be recovered quickly by anyone on the recovery team
How and when the plan is tested
so Kestrel knows the plan works before it is needed
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense
reject: Preventive measures such as antivirus or firewalls

questions.modelAnswer:
1. The plan should list which systems are restored first, such as delivery tracking, so drivers can keep delivering while less important systems wait.
2. It should name who is on the recovery team and how to contact them, so nobody wastes time working out who is responsible.

questions.context:
Priya has written this draft incident response policy:

1. Any member of staff who notices a problem emails the IT manager.
2. The IT manager decides whether it is an incident.
3. Affected computers are switched off immediately.
4. Systems are restored from the latest backup.
5. Once systems are working again, the incident is closed.
questions.question: Evaluate Priya's draft incident response policy.
traps: Evaluate means weigh strengths against weaknesses and reach a supported judgement.
Comment on the steps Priya actually wrote. A generic list of incident response stages will not reach Level 3.

markScheme.focus: The strengths and weaknesses of the five steps in Priya's draft, with a judgement on how effective the policy would be.
indicative: Strength: one clear reporting route, simple for staff to follow
Strength: someone with expertise (the IT manager) decides what counts as an incident
Weakness: email may be down or compromised during an incident; there is no phone or out-of-hours route
Weakness: single point of failure, as nobody covers if the IT manager is absent
Weakness: no severity levels or definition of an incident, so staff may not report
Weakness: switching off destroys volatile evidence in memory; isolating from the network would contain it and keep evidence
Weakness: restoring the latest backup may restore the malware too; there is no containment or eradication step to find the cause
Weakness: no communication plan for directors, customers, or the ICO within 72 hours for a personal data breach
Weakness: no incident log of actions taken, so nothing to learn from or show investigators
Weakness: no review or lessons learned before closing (Plan-Do-Check-Act), and the plan is never tested
Conclusion: a reasonable start but not effective yet; judge the most important changes

questions.modelAnswer:
Priya's draft has some strengths. Having one clear reporting route makes it easy for staff to raise a problem, and having the IT manager decide whether something is an incident means a person with expertise makes the call.

However, the policy has serious weaknesses. Reporting only by email will fail if the incident has taken down the email system or the attacker can read it, so staff need a phone number too. Everything depends on the IT manager, so nothing happens if she is on holiday or off sick.

Step 3 could make things worse. Switching computers off destroys evidence held in memory, such as running malware. Disconnecting them from the network would contain the incident and keep the evidence. Step 4 assumes the backup is clean, but if the malware was present before the last backup, restoring it brings the problem straight back. There is no step to find and remove the cause first.

The draft also says nothing about telling the directors or customers, or reporting a personal data breach to the ICO within 72 hours, even though the lost laptop shows this is a real risk. Finally, closing the incident as soon as systems work means there is no review of what went wrong, so the same incident could happen again.

Overall, the draft would help Kestrel react, but it would not contain an incident properly and could break the law on breach reporting. Adding containment, legal reporting, a deputy and a lessons-learned review would make it effective.

questions.question: Draw a network diagram for Lumen's new office. Your diagram should show how the devices are connected and include the security features the network needs. Annotate your diagram.
traps: The marks are for security features as well as devices. A diagram that only connects PCs to a switch will score low.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each feature your diagram shows, up to 6 marks.
points: Router connecting the office to the internet, with a firewall between the internet and the internal network
The web server for the client portal in a DMZ, separated from the internal network by a firewall
The 12 designers' PCs on a wired connection to a switch
The reception PC and printer connected to the network
Guest Wi-Fi from a WAP on a separate VLAN / network, with WPA2 or WPA3, so guests reach the internet only
Home workers' laptops connecting over the internet through a VPN to the firewall / VPN gateway
The file server on the internal network, not reachable from guest Wi-Fi
Annotations naming devices, connection types and security features
accept: Wired or wireless links where either would work
A single combined router/firewall device
reject: Guest Wi-Fi on the same network as the file server

questions.modelAnswer:
Internet → router → firewall. The firewall has three zones:
• DMZ: web server (client portal)
• Internal LAN: switch → 12 designer PCs (wired), file server, reception PC, printer
• Guest VLAN: WAP (WPA3) in the meeting room, internet access only
Home workers: laptop → internet → encrypted VPN tunnel → firewall/VPN gateway → file server.
Annotate each device, each link (wired / wireless / VPN) and each security feature.

questions.question: Explain **one** factor Lumen should consider when choosing the wireless access point for the meeting room.
traps: "Fast" or "secure" on its own is not a factor. Say what feature makes it so.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a factor and 1 more for explaining why it matters to Lumen, up to 2 marks.
points: Supports WPA3 / strong encryption
so clients' traffic cannot easily be intercepted or the key cracked
Supports multiple SSIDs / VLANs
so guest Wi-Fi can be kept separate from the staff network and file server
Range / coverage
so the signal covers the meeting room without reaching far outside the building
Number of users and bandwidth it supports
so several clients can download large design files at once
Power over Ethernet
so it can be placed on the ceiling without a nearby power socket
Cost
so it fits the budget for the office move
accept: Any other sensible factor with a linked reason
reject: "Fast", "secure" or "cheap" with no reason

questions.modelAnswer: The access point should support several SSIDs on separate VLANs, so guest Wi-Fi is kept apart from the staff network and clients cannot reach the file server.

questions.question: Explain **two** benefits to Lumen of segmenting its network, for example by using VLANs.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a benefit and 1 more for expanding it, up to 4 marks.
points: Guest devices are kept separate
so visiting clients cannot reach the file server or designers' PCs
Contains malware or an attack
because an infection on one segment cannot easily spread to the others
Different security rules for each segment
e.g. stricter firewall rules for the segment holding the file server
Better performance
because there is less broadcast traffic, so large design files transfer faster
Easier to manage and monitor
so unusual traffic on a segment is easier to spot
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense
reject: "More secure" with no explanation

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Guests in the meeting room would be on their own segment, so a client's laptop could not reach the file server holding other clients' designs.
2. If malware infected a designer's PC, segmentation would stop it spreading easily to reception or the servers.

questions.question: Evaluate whether Lumen should host the client portal on its own web server in a DMZ or use a cloud hosting provider.
traps: Weigh both options for Lumen, then commit to a recommendation that follows from your points.

markScheme.focus: Own web server in a DMZ against cloud hosting, for a small design studio's client portal.
indicative: Own server: full control over configuration and where client data is stored
Own server: the DMZ limits the damage if the web server is compromised, keeping attackers away from the file server
Own server: no monthly fee, but the hardware has to be bought, powered and replaced
Own server: Lumen must patch and secure it itself, which needs skills a design studio may not have
Own server: a power cut or broadband fault takes the portal offline; it is exposed to DDoS
Cloud: the provider handles patching, physical security and DDoS protection
Cloud: scalable and highly available, with providers' backup and recovery
Cloud: ongoing subscription cost and less control over the platform
Cloud: client data held by a third party, so there is GDPR to consider, an external services policy / contract, and where data is stored
Cloud: shared responsibility, as Lumen still has to manage accounts and passwords
Conclusion: a justified recommendation for Lumen

questions.modelAnswer:
Hosting the portal on its own server in a DMZ would give Lumen full control. It would decide exactly how the server is configured and know where clients' designs are stored. The DMZ is also a sensible design: if attackers broke into the web server they would still be separated from the file server and designers' PCs by the firewall.

However, Lumen is a small design studio and is unlikely to have staff who can patch and harden a public web server. Any missed update would leave the portal exposed. The portal would also go offline whenever the office loses power or broadband, and a DDoS attack could take it down. Lumen would also have to buy and replace the hardware.

A cloud hosting provider would take on patching, physical security and DDoS protection, and the portal would stay available even if the office had problems. It can scale up when many clients download large files at once. The downsides are a monthly cost, less control, and the fact that clients' designs would be held by a third party. Lumen would need a contract and an external services policy covering how the provider protects the data and where it is stored under GDPR, and it would still be responsible for strong passwords on client accounts.

Overall, cloud hosting is the better choice for Lumen. Its biggest risk is an unpatched or unavailable server, and a provider is far better placed to manage that than a small studio, as long as Lumen checks the provider's data protection terms.

questions.question: Explain **one** reason why the investigator should create a forensic image of Alex's laptop drive rather than examining the original drive.
traps: Three marks for one reason: give the reason, justify it, then expand the justification.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a reason, 1 for justifying it, and 1 for expanding the justification, up to 3 marks.
points: To preserve the original evidence
because examining the original can change data such as timestamps or metadata
so the evidence could be challenged and may not be accepted in court or a tribunal
So the analysis can be repeated
because the image can be copied and examined as many times as needed
so another examiner can check and verify the findings
To prove the copy is exact
because hash values of the original and the image can be compared
showing nothing was altered, which makes the evidence reliable
To recover deleted data
because a bit-for-bit image copies every sector, not just visible files
so files Alex deleted after copying could still be found
reject: "So you don't break it" with no link to evidence

questions.modelAnswer: Working on an image preserves the original evidence, because even opening files on the original drive can change their timestamps. If the original were changed, Alex's lawyer could argue the evidence had been tampered with, so it might not be accepted.

questions.context: Before calling anyone in, Brightwater's IT technician, Sam, examined the laptop himself. He switched it on, logged in with the administrator account and searched for files with "customer" in the name. He copied the files he found to a USB stick from his desk drawer. When he had finished, he wrote a short note of what he had found.
questions.question: Evaluate the way Sam examined Alex's laptop.
traps: Judge Sam's actions against forensic procedure, and say what the effect is on the evidence, not just what he did wrong.

markScheme.focus: Sam's actions measured against forensic procedure, and their effect on whether the evidence can be relied on.
indicative: Strengths: acted quickly, found relevant files, and made some record of what he did
Switching on and logging in changes data (logs, timestamps, last-accessed dates), contaminating the evidence
No write-blocker and no forensic image: he worked on the original
No hash values, so nothing proves the files are unchanged
Copied files to an unchecked USB stick, which could alter or contaminate them
Notes written afterwards, not contemporaneous, with no times or step-by-step actions
No chain of custody record of who handled the laptop and when
No photographs of the laptop's state before he started
Searching only for "customer" misses renamed, compressed or deleted files and the cloud upload evidence
Not trained and not independent, so the evidence may be challenged in court or a tribunal
Conclusion: well meant but it has weakened the evidence; say what should have happened

questions.modelAnswer:
Sam acted quickly and did find files that may be relevant, and he made a note of his findings, so there is some record of what happened.

However, his method has seriously weakened the evidence. Switching the laptop on and logging in changes data on the drive, including log files and last-accessed times, so it is now harder to show what Alex did rather than what Sam did. He worked on the original drive instead of using a write-blocker and taking a forensic image, and he took no hash values, so he cannot prove the files are unchanged. Copying files to a USB stick from his drawer could also have altered them.

His record-keeping is weak too. He wrote a short note afterwards rather than contemporaneous notes with times and actions, and there is no chain of custody showing who had the laptop and when. A lawyer could argue that the evidence was planted or changed.

His search was also limited. Looking only for file names containing "customer" would miss renamed, compressed or deleted files, and it ignores the most important evidence: the uploads to Alex's personal cloud account.

Overall, although Sam meant well, his examination was not forensically sound, and the evidence may not stand up if Brightwater takes legal action. He should have isolated and bagged the laptop, recorded its handling, and passed it to a trained investigator who would image it through a write-blocker and verify the image with hash values.

questions.question: Evaluate whether Brightwater should use its own IT staff or an external digital forensics company to investigate this incident.
traps: 12 marks: cover both options in depth, link every point to Brightwater, and end with a judgement that follows from what you argued.
Consider the seriousness of the incident as well as cost.

markScheme.focus: In-house IT staff against an external forensics company for a suspected theft of customer data that may go to court.
indicative: In-house: cheaper and can start immediately
In-house: knows Brightwater's systems, logs and network well
In-house: keeps confidential customer data inside the company
In-house: usually lacks forensic training and tools (write-blockers, imaging software)
In-house: may know Alex, giving a possible conflict of interest or bias
In-house: evidence may be challenged in court; the investigation takes time away from normal work
External: trained, experienced investigators who follow recognised procedures
External: proper tools, hash verification and chain of custody
External: independent, so findings are more credible and they can act as expert witnesses
External: can produce a formal security report
External: costly and may take time to arrange
External: confidential data shared with a third party, so a contract / NDA and an external services policy are needed (GDPR processor)
External: does not know Brightwater's systems as well
Wider: possible personal data breach, so the ICO must be told within 72 hours; police may be involved; Sam's actions have already weakened the evidence
Possible combination: IT staff secure and preserve evidence (isolate, record, keep logs); external specialists do the analysis
Conclusion: a justified recommendation

questions.modelAnswer:
Using Brightwater's own IT staff has clear advantages. They could start straight away and it would cost little, which matters if customer data is still being shared. They also know the company's systems, so they could quickly find the network logs that show the uploads to Alex's cloud account. Keeping the investigation in-house also means confidential customer data is not passed to another company.

However, the IT staff are not forensic investigators. Sam's examination shows the risk: by switching the laptop on and copying files without a write-blocker, hash values or a chain of custody, he has already weakened the evidence. In-house staff are also likely to have worked with Alex, so a defence lawyer could argue that the investigation was biased. Running the investigation would also pull the IT team away from their normal work.

An external digital forensics company would bring trained investigators and specialist tools. They would image the phone and laptop through write-blockers, verify each image with hash values and keep a full chain of custody, so the evidence is far more likely to be accepted. Because they are independent, their findings carry more weight, and they can write a formal report and act as expert witnesses if the case goes to court.

The drawbacks are cost and the time it takes to agree a contract, and Brightwater would have to share confidential customer data with a third party. That means it needs a contract or non-disclosure agreement and must follow its external services policy so the company handles the data in line with GDPR. The external team would also need time to learn Brightwater's systems.

The seriousness of the incident is the deciding factor. Customer records may have been stolen, which is a personal data breach that must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours, and Brightwater may take legal action. Evidence that is challenged in court is worth very little.

Overall, Brightwater should use an external forensics company. The IT staff still have a role: they should immediately preserve the network logs, stop using the devices and record who has handled them, then hand over to the specialists. This combines the speed and system knowledge of the in-house team with the independence and forensic rigour the case needs.

questions.question: State what is meant by tailgating.
questions.modelAnswer: Following an authorised person through a secure/controlled door to gain entry without using your own credentials.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a correct definition.
points: Following an authorised person through a secure / controlled door without using your own pass or credentials
accept: Piggybacking described in the same way
reject: "Following someone" with no mention of getting into a secure area

questions.question: Describe the difference between a DoS and a DDoS attack.
questions.modelAnswer: A DoS attack floods a target from a single computer to make it unavailable (1). A DDoS uses many computers (a botnet) at once, so it is much harder to block (1).
traps: "Describe the difference": you need something about each attack, not just a definition of one.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: A DoS attack comes from a single computer / source
A DDoS attack comes from many computers at once, often a botnet
A DDoS is harder to block because traffic comes from many different addresses
Both flood a target with traffic / requests so it becomes unavailable to genuine users
reject: Saying one is "bigger" with no reason

questions.question: Explain one way trusted computing can help secure a network against threats.
questions.modelAnswer: Trusted computing reduces the risk of cyber-attacks (1) because it provides an extra layer of protection / verification before access is granted, increasing security (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.
points: Checks that hardware and software have not been tampered with before they run (e.g. secure boot / TPM)
so malware such as a rootkit cannot load when the device starts
Stores encryption keys in a TPM chip on the device
so keys cannot easily be copied off the machine by an attacker
Verifies a device's identity / health before it can join the network
so untrusted or compromised devices are kept off the network
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense

questions.question: Explain the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup.
questions.modelAnswer: A full backup copies all selected data every time it runs (1). An incremental backup only copies the data that has changed since the last backup, making it faster and using less storage (1).
traps: Say what each backup copies. "Incremental is faster" alone does not explain the difference.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: A full backup copies all the selected data every time it runs
An incremental backup only copies data that has changed since the last backup
Incremental backups are quicker and use less storage
Restoring from incrementals needs the last full backup plus every incremental since

questions.question: Describe one digital threat to an organisation's network and an appropriate countermeasure for it.
questions.modelAnswer: Phishing: an email pretending to be from a trusted source tricks staff into giving away their login (1), letting the attacker into the network (1). Countermeasure: security-awareness training plus email filtering (1), so staff recognise and report phishing and most of it never arrives (1).
traps: One threat only. Describe how it works, then a countermeasure and how it reduces that threat.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a threat, 1 for how it affects the network, 1 for a countermeasure, 1 for how the countermeasure reduces the threat, up to 4 marks.
points: Phishing
fake emails trick staff into giving away logins, letting attackers into the network
staff training / email filtering
so staff recognise and report phishing and most never reaches inboxes
Ransomware / malware
malicious software encrypts or damages files across the network
anti-malware software kept up to date, plus offline backups
so infections are detected and blocked, and data can be restored without paying
DoS / DDoS attack
floods servers with traffic so genuine users cannot connect
firewall rules / DDoS protection service
so attack traffic is filtered out before it reaches the server
Brute-force password attack
tries many passwords until one works and the account is taken over
account lockout and MFA
so repeated guesses are blocked and a cracked password alone is not enough
SQL injection
malicious SQL in a web form lets the attacker read or change the database
input validation / parameterised queries
so input is treated as data and cannot run as a command
accept: Any other valid digital threat and matching countermeasure
reject: Physical threats such as theft (the question asks for a digital threat)

questions.question: Explain why MAC address filtering only provides medium-level security for a Wi-Fi network.
questions.modelAnswer: MAC address filtering only allows listed devices onto the network (1), but a MAC address can be spoofed (faked) by an attacker who copies an allowed address, so it should not be relied on alone (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.
points: Only devices with a listed MAC address can connect
but MAC addresses can be spoofed by copying an allowed address, so an attacker can still get on
MAC addresses are sent unencrypted
so an attacker can capture an allowed address with a wireless sniffer and reuse it
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense

questions.question: State two rights that individuals have over their personal data under GDPR.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: the right to access their own data; to be informed how it is used; to have data corrected, removed or restricted; to object to processing; to data portability; not to be subject to a solely automated decision.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Right to be informed about how their data is used
Right of access to the data held about them
Right to have inaccurate data corrected (rectification)
Right to have data deleted (erasure / to be forgotten)
Right to restrict processing
Right to data portability
Right to object to processing
Rights about automated decision-making and profiling
reject: GDPR principles, e.g. "data must be accurate" (those are duties on the organisation, not rights)

questions.question: Describe how an SQL injection attack works.
questions.modelAnswer: An attacker enters malicious SQL code into an input field on a website, such as a login or search box (1). If the input is not properly validated or sanitised, the database executes this code as part of a query (1). This allows the attacker to view, change or delete data they should not have access to, such as user credentials (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 3 marks.
points: The attacker types malicious SQL code into an input field, e.g. a login or search box
The input is not validated / sanitised
So the database runs the attacker's code as part of a query
The attacker can read, change or delete data they should not reach, e.g. usernames and passwords
Can be used to bypass a login, e.g. ' OR '1'='1

questions.question: Explain one method of preventing SQL injection.
questions.modelAnswer: Use input validation / parameterised queries (1) so that user input is treated only as data and cannot be executed as SQL commands, preventing malicious code from running (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.
points: Parameterised queries / prepared statements
so user input is always treated as data and can never run as an SQL command
Input validation / sanitisation
so characters such as quotes and SQL keywords are rejected or removed before reaching the database
Least privilege for the database account
so even a successful injection cannot delete tables or read other data
accept: Mix and match an identification with any expansion if it makes sense

questions.question: A network diagram needs a device added to provide secure internet access. Identify the device and state where it should be connected.
questions.modelAnswer: A firewall (1), connected between the router/internet connection and the internal network (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for the device and 1 for where it is connected, up to 2 marks.
points: Firewall
between the router / internet connection and the internal network
accept: A router with a built-in firewall, placed at the internet connection

questions.question: Describe how a VPN allows a remote worker to connect securely to their organisation.
questions.modelAnswer: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between the worker's device and the organisation's network over the internet (1). Intercepted data cannot be read (1), so the worker can safely use internal files and systems as if on-site (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 3 marks.
points: Creates a secure tunnel between the worker's device and the organisation over the internet
Data in the tunnel is encrypted, so intercepted traffic cannot be read
The user is authenticated before the tunnel is set up
The worker can use internal files and systems as if they were in the office

questions.question: When configuring a DHCP server, the administrator enters the default gateway address. State two other pieces of configuration information that must be entered.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: the range of available IP addresses; the lease length/time; reserved/fixed IP addresses; the server address.
traps: The default gateway is already given, so it earns nothing.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: The range / pool of IP addresses to hand out
The subnet mask
The DNS server address
The lease time
Reserved / fixed addresses for particular devices
Excluded addresses

questions.question: Describe one method of attacking a network by exploiting DHCP.
questions.modelAnswer: The attacker sets up a rogue DHCP server (1). DHCP has no authentication, so devices may accept its settings instead of the real server's (1). It hands out a malicious gateway or DNS server, sending victims' traffic through the attacker to intercept or alter (1).
traps: One method only. Describe it in three linked steps.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for the method, 1 for how it works, 1 for the result, up to 3 marks.
points: A rogue / fake DHCP server is set up on the network
DHCP has no authentication, so devices may accept its settings instead of the real server's
it hands out a malicious gateway or DNS server, so the attacker can intercept or redirect traffic
DHCP starvation
the attacker floods the server with requests using fake MAC addresses until the address pool runs out
genuine devices cannot get an IP address, a denial of service (often before a rogue server takes over)

questions.question: Staff and guest Wi-Fi both connect to a single switch, which is a security risk. Describe how the network should be changed to reduce this risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Separate staff and guest traffic, e.g. on different VLANs or switches (1). Give guests internet access only (1), so they cannot reach staff devices or data and an attacker cannot move across the network (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 3 marks.
points: Separate staff and guest traffic, e.g. different VLANs or a separate switch
Give guests internet access only
Firewall rules between the two segments
So guests cannot reach staff devices, servers or data
And an attacker on the guest network cannot move across to the staff network

questions.question: Explain the difference between an intranet and an extranet.
questions.modelAnswer: An intranet is a private network accessible only to an organisation's own staff (1). An extranet extends controlled access to selected external parties such as suppliers or partners (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: An intranet is private and can only be used by the organisation's own staff
An extranet gives controlled access to selected outsiders, e.g. suppliers, partners or customers

questions.question: Explain one vulnerability of a wireless access point (WAP).
questions.modelAnswer: A WAP broadcasts radio signals that pass outside the building/through walls (1), so an attacker in a public area could intercept traffic or attempt to connect to the network (1).

so an attacker nearby could intercept traffic or try to connect

can be cracked quickly, letting an attacker read traffic or join the network
Default admin password left unchanged
so anyone could log in and change its settings
A rogue / evil-twin access point copying the real network name
tricks users into connecting so their traffic can be captured

questions.question: A password policy already covers length, sharing and uniqueness. Give two other sections a password policy should contain.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: password expiry/minimum age; lockout after failed login attempts; deny list of common/weak passwords; rules on storage/use of password managers.

A list of banned common or weak passwords

Complexity: a mix of character types
What to do if you think a password is compromised
Use of MFA alongside passwords

questions.question: Explain one advantage of staff using a password manager.
questions.modelAnswer: A password manager lets staff use long, unique, random passwords for every account (1) without having to remember them, reducing the risk of weak or reused passwords being cracked (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.

without remembering them, so weak or reused passwords are not cracked

questions.question: Explain one disadvantage of staff using a password manager.
questions.modelAnswer: If the master password is compromised, an attacker gains access to ALL stored passwords at once (1), creating a single point of failure that could expose every account (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.
points: Single point of failure: the master password
if it is stolen, the attacker gets every stored password at once
If the master password is forgotten
staff may be locked out of all their accounts
The password manager itself could be breached or have a vulnerability

questions.question: Describe the main stages of a cyber security incident response.
questions.modelAnswer: First, triage and escalation — the incident is assessed and the right people are alerted (1). Then the main response — analysis, containment to stop it spreading, mitigation and recovery of systems (1). Finally, the incident is reviewed, reported and closed so lessons can be learned (1).
traps: Describe the stages in order. A list of single words will not get full marks.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 3 marks.
points: Triage / identify and assess the incident and escalate it to the right people
Contain it to stop it spreading, e.g. isolate affected systems
Eradicate / mitigate the cause, e.g. remove malware, close the vulnerability
Recover systems and data, e.g. restore from clean backups
Review, report and close: record what happened and learn lessons

questions.question: Explain why an investigator takes a physical image of an entire drive instead of a targeted image of specific files.
questions.modelAnswer: A physical image copies the entire drive including deleted, temporary and system files (1), so it captures more potential evidence that a targeted image of only specific files might miss (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for a linked expansion, up to 2 marks.
points: A physical image copies the whole drive, including deleted, hidden and unallocated space

It does not rely on the investigator guessing which files matter
so evidence in unexpected places, e.g. renamed files, is still collected

questions.question: Describe the process for creating a forensic image of a device's drive.
questions.modelAnswer: Connect the drive through a write-blocker so the original can't change (1). Make a bit-for-bit copy with forensic imaging software (1). Hash both the original and the copy to prove they are identical (1).

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 3 marks.

Make a bit-for-bit copy using forensic imaging software

Record each step / keep the chain of custody

questions.question: Explain which type of log file is likely to contain evidence that a password manager has been compromised.

because it records login attempts and access, so unusual or failed logins to the password manager would show up
Application log for the password manager

questions.question: Explain why a seized mobile device should be placed in a Faraday bag.
questions.modelAnswer: A Faraday bag blocks all wireless signals to and from the device (1), preventing it from being remotely wiped or altered, which preserves the evidence stored on it (1).

It stops new data arriving on the phone

questions.question: State two requirements for ensuring forensic evidence is reliable.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: no action should change data on the device; collection by a competent person; a full record/trail of all actions (chain of custody); documenting who is responsible for each decision.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: No action should change the data on the device
Anyone who accesses original data must be competent and able to explain what they did
A full record / audit trail of every action is kept (chain of custody)
The person in charge is responsible for making sure these rules are followed
